title: Ethiopian Sesame Honey Candy
localName: ሰሊጥ ማር ቅቤ — Selit Mar Qibe
community: All of Ethiopia — the ancient sesame-honey confection
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Sesame Honey Candy — white and black sesame seeds combined, toasted, and caramelised in Ethiopian honey with a touch of cardamom, poured into a slab and broken into irregular pieces. The premium version of sesame brittle — using both seed colours and cardamom for greater complexity.
longDesc: Sesame honey candy is the refined version of the sesame brittle (ETH174) — using both white and black sesame seeds and adding cardamom to the honey caramel produces a confection of greater visual beauty and flavour depth. Made for celebrations and given as gifts.
equipment: Lined baking sheet or oiled marble surface
steps: Toast both sesame seed varieties together in a dry pan 2—3 minutes until white seeds are golden.
Add honey, sugar, cardamom, and salt to the pan.
Stir over medium heat continuously 6—8 minutes until the mixture turns deep amber.
Test: drop into cold water — it should form a hard ball (hard ball stage, 120°C).
Spread as thin as possible with an oiled spatula.
chefTips: The black sesame seeds provide visual contrast and a slightly more bitter, nutty note.
The cardamom in the hot honey is the Ethiopian signature.
Work quickly at the pouring stage — this sets faster than sesame brittle.
commonMistakes: Not reaching hard ball stage — sticky.
Too slow spreading — sets before thin.
cookingScience: See ETH174 for brittle science. Hard ball stage (120°C) produces a different sugar matrix than hard crack (150°C) — the candy is chewier than brittle but still firm. The two sesame varieties provide different Maillard browning profiles (black sesame being already dark, white sesame browning gold) creating visual interest.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian sesame from Tigray and Humera — world-class sesame.
healthBenefits: Sesame — very high calcium, zinc, and healthy fats.
culturalNote: Ethiopian sesame honey candy with cardamom is the celebration gift — made in large batches for Ethiopian New Year (Enkutatash), for Easter, and for weddings, wrapped in cloth and distributed among guests. Its black-and-white sesame appearance makes it visually distinctive.
